keyPhrases.text: I'd like to make an appointment.

keyPhrases.de: Können Sie das bitte langsamer sagen?
keyPhrases.text: Could you please say that more slowly?
I have a headache and a fever.
Three times a day after meals.

subtitles.text: You're sick. You have to see a doctor. But … in German?
Oh no. Last time at the doctor's I said: „Ich bin Kopfschmerzen.“ (I am headache.)
That's exactly why we're here today. You'll go through a whole doctor's visit – from the first call to the prescription.
And in every situation we ask you: What do you say?
And you only have five seconds!
You call the doctor's office. Someone answers.
Dr. Yilmaz's practice, Schulz speaking. How can I help you?
What do you say?
A: I want doctor. Now.
B: Good morning, I'd like to make an appointment.
C: Hello, I'm sick. Bye.
B! „Ich möchte gern …“ (I'd like …) is polite and always works.
„Ich will“ (I want) quickly sounds rude on the phone.
Good morning, I'd like to make an appointment.
Sure. Does ten o'clock today work?
Repeat after me!
I'd like to make an appointment.
You arrive at the practice. At the reception they ask you:
Do you have your health insurance card with you?
What do you say?
A: No, I am insured not.
B: Yes, I'm hungry.
C: Yes, here is my card.
C! The „Versichertenkarte“ – some people also say „Gesundheitskarte“ or „Krankenkassenkarte“.
It's always the same card. Take it to every doctor's visit.
Yes, here is my card.
Thank you.
Repeat after me!
Yes, here is my card.
The woman speaks very fast. You don't understand everything.
Please fill out the form and then take a seat in the waiting room.
What do you say?
A: Excuse me, could you please say that more slowly?
B: What?
C: I'll take the seat with me.
A! „Was?“ (What?) sounds rude. This question saves you everywhere: „Können Sie das bitte langsamer sagen?“
Shorter works too: „Wie bitte?“ (Pardon?)
Excuse me, could you please say that more slowly?
Of course. Please fill out this form. Then wait over there in the waiting room.
Repeat after me!
Could you please say that more slowly?
You're in the consulting room with the doctor. He asks:
Hello. So, what seems to be the problem?
What do you say?
A: Nothing is wrong with me, thanks.
B: I have a headache and a fever.
C: I am headache.
B! Careful: „Was fehlt Ihnen?“ doesn't mean „What are you missing?“ but „What's your problem?“
If you say „Mir fehlt nichts“, you're healthy – and actually in the wrong place at the doctor's.
I have a headache and a fever.
Oh, I'm sorry to hear that.
Repeat after me!
I have a headache and a fever.
Do you also have stomach pain? Where does it hurt?
Your stomach hurts. What do you say?
A: I do hurt in the stomach.
B: The stomach is hurt.
C: Here, my stomach hurts.
C! This is how it works: body part plus „tut weh“ (hurts). For more than one: „Meine Füße tun weh.“ (My feet hurt.)
Here, my stomach hurts.
Repeat after me!
My stomach hurts.
My feet hurt.
How long have you had these symptoms?
What do you say?
A: Before three days long.
B: For three day.
C: For three days.
C! After „seit“ (since/for) comes the dative – that's why „Tagen“ has an n. Same with „seit einer Woche“
(for a week), „seit gestern“ (since yesterday).
For three days.
Repeat after me!
For three days.
For a week.
Let me listen to your chest. Please take off your top.
What do you do now?
A: You take off your sweater and T-shirt.
B: You take off your trousers.
C: You go home – you're free, after all.
So … C, right? I'm free – I'm going home!
No, Leo. A! The „Oberkörper“ is the upper part of the body. „Frei machen“ here means: take your clothes off.
Then you'll often hear: „Tief einatmen … und ausatmen.“ (Breathe in deeply … and breathe out.)
Breathe in deeply … and breathe out. Good.
Repeat after me!
breathe in – breathe out
Are you allergic to anything?
What do you say?
A: Yes, I'm allergic for penicillin.
B: Yes, I'm allergic to penicillin.
C: I don't like penicillin very much.
B! You're allergic „gegen“ something. And if you have no allergy: „Nein, ich habe keine Allergien.“
(No, I don't have any allergies.)
Yes, I'm allergic to penicillin.
Good that you told me. Then you'll get something else.
Repeat after me!
I'm allergic to penicillin.
I don't have any allergies.
You can't work tomorrow. The doctor asks:
Do you need a sick note?
What do you say?
A: No, I write myself.
B: Yes, I write sick.
C: Yes, please. For my employer.
C! The „Krankschreibung“ (sick note) shows: you're sick and can't work.
Important: still tell your employer yourself – ideally on the first day, early in the morning.
Yes, please. For my employer.
I'll sign you off sick until Friday.
Repeat after me!
I need a sick note.
I'll write you a prescription. Take the tablets three times a day after meals.
Listen carefully! When do you take the tablets?
A: Once a day, before going to sleep.
B: Morning, noon and evening – after meals.
C: Three times a day – before meals.
B! „Dreimal täglich“ means three times a day. And „nach dem Essen“
– so first eat, then take the tablet.
Thank you very much. Goodbye!
Get well soon!
„Gute Besserung“ – that's what you say to sick people. It means: get well soon!
Repeat after me!
Three times a day after meals.
Get well soon!
And if the practice is closed? Remember two numbers.
116 117: the medical on-call service – when you need a doctor at night or at the weekend, but it's not an emergency.
And 112: the emergency number – for ambulance and fire brigade, for example after an accident or if you have severe shortness of breath.
In class you learn nice sentences. But what do Germans really say?
I have a sore throat.
My throat is scratchy.
I am sick.
It's got me. (I've come down with something.)
I caught an infection.
I've picked something up.
I am very tired and weak.
I'm totally worn out.
I have back pain.
My back is playing up.
Brrr, I am so cold!
Leo … you're not a cold person. You mean: „Mir ist kalt.“ (I feel cold.)
And careful: „Mir ist schlecht“ doesn't mean „I'm not doing well“.
It means: I feel sick, I might throw up.
Flu or cold? A runny nose and a cough is usually a cold („Erkältung“).
The flu („Grippe“) is much worse: high fever, you stay in bed.
And now everything once more. The ten most important sentences. Repeat after me!
I'd like to make an appointment.
Here is my card.
Could you please say that more slowly?
I have a headache and a fever.
My stomach hurts.
For three days.
I'm allergic to penicillin.
I need a sick note.
Three times a day after meals.
Get well soon!
Which situation was the hardest for you? Write it in the comments!
Next time we're going to the authorities. I really need help there.
See you soon at LilyLingua!
